paras: The killing of Posey Drew was the fatal stabbing of Drew, a Black dance-house keeper, at the door of his house on Cary Street in Richmond, Virginia, on the night of April 16, 1881, by a member of a party of white youths from Manchester. A coroner's jury found that John Bowen struck the blow with his brother Charles as accessory, and a Hustings Court jury convicted John Bowen and sentenced him to three years in the penitentiary, while Charles was acquitted. Most of the coverage came from the Richmond Daily Dispatch, while a wire report printed elsewhere called the attackers unknown.

Drew, about forty, kept a dance-house at 1807 east Cary Street, in the quarter known as "Cash Corner." A Richmond dispatch to the Chicago Daily Tribune called the area "one of the lowest portions of the city" and said Drew's bar fronted on the dock with a sailors' dance-house behind it. The Dispatch wrote that, "strange as it may seem," Drew was regarded as quiet and well-behaved, and that he was "quite popular" among the city's Black residents.

About 8 o'clock that Saturday evening a party came to the house, apparently for a dance, and Drew objected to admitting one of the boys because he was too young. Testifying at the inquest, Charles Bowen named the party as himself, his brother John, Jim Butler, George Binn and Michael Binn, all white, and said Drew had told them to pay ten cents or leave. By his account, after some of the group jostled a Black man at the door, one of the party handed another a pocket-knife and Drew was stabbed in the breast.

A neighbor, Lizzie Kelly, and Fannie Chalkley, who was in the house, both testified that Charles Bowen held the knife, Kelly recalling that a man on the sidewalk had told Drew, "We got your protection here; we got your age." Drew died on the floor within about ten minutes, and the post-mortem found the wound had entered his right lung.

That night police arrested William Gilliam, and Charles Bowen surrendered, saying the blow was struck over his shoulder by someone he did not know. At its second session the coroner's jury found that Drew died "at the hands of John Bowen" with Charles Bowen as accessory.

John Bowen, about nineteen, hid for several days in Chesterfield, by his own account in a stable where a sweetheart fed him, before taking a train to Lynchburg. A Lynchburg officer who had read the Dispatch's account arrested him on April 23, and he was said to have confessed. At the Police Court on April 26 an officer testified that Bowen admitted the stabbing but claimed self-defence, saying Drew had raised a stick to strike him.

The Police Justice sent John and Charles Bowen and George Binn to the grand jury, which indicted all three for murder on May 2, while Butler and Michael Binn, who was under fourteen, were discharged. On May 6 a Hustings Court jury found John Bowen guilty and fixed his term at three years, and the next day Charles Bowen was tried and acquitted. Bowen went to the penitentiary on May 14 still claiming self-defence, and in August a petition circulated in Manchester asking the governor to pardon him; no result of the petition appears in the coverage.

Coverage was mainly local: the Richmond Daily Dispatch printed the first detailed report, long columns of inquest testimony, and items on each later step of the case. Its first headline said Drew was "stabbed to death for refusing admittance to a minor," and it called his house a resort of "the most degraded of both sexes and color" while noting his quiet reputation.

Outside Richmond, a wire dispatch printed in Chicago and Wilmington said a white man and two boys stabbed Drew after he "politely" refused them whisky, and that their names were unknown. The Staunton Spectator called it a "fatal stabbing affray," a Daily Republican digest said Drew died "trying to eject several whites," and the National Republican and the Virginia Star carried later developments.

When Bowen went to prison, the Dispatch reported that many believed he had taken the blame to shield another, a theory it called "too Damon-and-Pythias-like," and its year-end chronicle listed Drew as stabbed "by Charles Bowen." None of the reports gave a racial motive, though the wire and digest versions identified the attackers as white and Drew as "a mulatto."

The wire gave a man and two boys refused whisky, the Dispatch a man and three youths refused admission for one boy, and Charles Bowen five companions asked to pay ten cents. Two inquest witnesses named Charles Bowen as the man with the knife, but the coroner's jury, John Bowen's reported admission and the trial jury placed the blow on John. The Virginia Star listed Michael rather than George Binn as sent to the grand jury, but the indictment named George.

reader.title: Killing of Posey Drew
bases: A homicide committed by one member of a small party of white youths and a young man during a quarrel at the door of a Black-run dance-house over admitting an underage boy, prosecuted to conviction, with no racial motive stated in any report (A2, A4, A5, A16).

The local Dispatch (A2, A4) and an independent Richmond wire dispatch (A1, A6) agree that Drew was stabbed to death at his house on Cary Street on the night of April 16 by one of a white party, and the inquest, hearing and trial (A5, A13, A16) confirm it.

accounts.label: Richmond wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A white man and two boys entered Drew's barroom; when he politely refused to sell whisky to boys, the three jumped on him and stabbed him to death; their names were unknown.

accounts.label: Dispatch first report (Fannie Chalkley)
accounts.gist: A man and three youths came for a dance; Drew refused one boy as too young; after Chalkley pushed two boys out, the oldest youth handed the man a knife and Drew was cut.

accounts.label: Charles Bowen at the inquest
accounts.gist: Five white companions went to the house; after a jostle with a Black man at the door, an unnamed stout, left-handed youth of about sixteen stabbed Drew, who had done nothing to provoke it.

accounts.label: Lizzie Kelly and Fannie Chalkley at the inquest
accounts.gist: A boy handed Charles Bowen something like a knife and Bowen made the stabbing motion; Chalkley saw him with the knife raised.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Drew died by stabbing at the hands of John Bowen, with Charles Bowen accessory.

accounts.label: John Bowen's statement (via Officer Garthright)
accounts.gist: He stabbed Drew in self-defence because Drew had a stick raised to strike him.

framing.detail: The Dispatch headlined Drew 'stabbed to death for refusing admittance to a minor', called his house a resort of 'the most degraded of both sexes and color', yet said he was quiet and well-behaved, and covered the prosecution in detail.
The Richmond wire, in Chicago and Wilmington, set the killing in 'one of the lowest portions of the city' but said Drew refused the boys 'politely'.
The Staunton Spectator called it a 'Fatal Stabbing Affray'; a Daily Republican digest under 'A Chapter of Violence' said Drew died trying to eject 'several whites'.
The Virginia Star reported the Police Court hearing as 'The Posey Drew Murder Case', noting that a local lawyer would assist the prosecution.
